prompt: What primarily distinguishes an intermediate-difficulty HTB/TryHackMe box from an easy one?
choices: Intermediate boxes require chaining multiple lower-severity findings together rather than exploiting one obvious CVE
Intermediate boxes always run Windows Server
Intermediate boxes never require privilege escalation
Intermediate boxes always involve a web application

prompt: A service on an intermediate target returns a generic banner with no version string. What is the correct next step?
choices: Give up on that service and brute-force every other open port instead
Fingerprint it manually using response headers, error page wording, and default behavior, then correlate with known framework/CVE fingerprints
Assume it is running the newest version and try the latest public CVE
Re-run nmap -sV repeatedly until it eventually returns a version

prompt: Why does time-boxing each attack avenue (e.g., 20-30 minutes) matter on intermediate-difficulty targets?
choices: It is a scoring rule enforced automatically by the platform
It prevents red herrings and rabbit holes from consuming the entire available time
It is required so nmap scans do not time out
It guarantees the first vulnerability found is always the correct path

prompt: In a Kerberoasting workflow against your own AD lab, what does a hash extracted with impacket-GetUserSPNs and cracked with `hashcat -m 13100` actually represent?
choices: The domain administrator's NTLM hash
A TGS-REP (service ticket) encrypted with the target service account's own password hash
The KRBTGT account's secret key
An AS-REP pre-authentication hash

prompt: Per the platform write-up policy conventions covered earlier in this track, when is it acceptable to publish a full step-by-step write-up of an HTB or TryHackMe machine?
choices: At any time, as long as the platform is credited
Only after the platform has officially retired that specific machine, confirmed before publishing
Only if the machine has fewer than 100 solves
Only if the write-up omits the machine's name

prompt: What is the primary purpose of running a tool like linPEAS or winPEAS after obtaining an initial low-privileged shell?
choices: It automatically grants root or administrator access
It performs the full network reconnaissance for other hosts
It enumerates common local privilege-escalation vectors (SUID binaries, sudo misconfigurations, writable cron jobs, stored credentials) for manual follow-up
It cracks any password hashes found on disk

prompt: BloodHound shows that a cracked service account in your lab has GenericAll rights over the Domain Admins group. What does this mean?
choices: Nothing exploitable, since GenericAll only applies to organizational units
A viable privilege-escalation path: that right lets the account add itself (or another controlled principal) directly into Domain Admins
BloodHound misreported the edge and it should be ignored
The finding only matters if the account also has local administrator rights on the DC

prompt: In a PTES-style report adapted into a retired-machine CTF write-up, what should the Scope section include that a standard client-engagement report would not?
choices: Nothing; the Scope section is written identically either way
A statement that this is independent training practice (not an authorized client engagement), the platform name, and confirmation the machine is retired
The client organization's legal name and signed authorization letter
A non-disclosure agreement
